title: For the 17th or 18th time, Putin promised to take Donetsk “in a few months” – Zelenskyy
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian President Vladimir Putin has again told US officials that Russia can capture Ukraine’s Donetsk Oblast within several months, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Speaking to the UN General Assembly on 24 September, Zelenskyy said this was the latest in a long series of similar promises as Russia has spent nearly five years trying to seize the region. He said Putin has made such promises 17 or 18 times, repeatedly pushing the deadline further back. He contrasted those promises with Russia’s heavy battlefield losses and relatively limited territorial gains. Russia has paid a huge price for its Donetsk offensive Zelenskyy said Russian forces suffered 248,964 troops killed or severely wounded between January and August 2026. He said Russia had captured only slightly more than 1,000 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this year, while Ukraine had already liberated a significant portion of those gains. Zelenskyy presented the figures as the human cost of Putin’s continued attempt to seize Donetsk, arguing that Russia is paying an enormous price for relatively limited territorial gains. “Always the same: ‘Just a few more months,’” Zelenskyy said, adding that Putin would again fail to meet his latest deadline. The Russian offensive is also facing a recent setback in northern Donetsk. Ukraine launched Operation Vivaldi in September to clear Russian infiltrators and retake ground near Lyman, disrupting Russia’s plan to encircle the fortified cities of the Donetsk “Fortress Belt.” Ukrainian forces have reported retaking several settlements and clearing up to 125 square kilometers in the operation, although the full scope of the offensive remains undisclosed. Explore further Ukraine retakes ground in a region Russia has fought for years to capture. “Vivaldi” is only getting started but is already “one of the most important victories for Ukraine in 2026” Zelenskyy also warned that Russia’s ambitions extend beyond Donetsk. After saying Putin would again fail to capture the region, he said Russia would continue seeking other Ukrainian cities, naming Odesa, Kharkiv and Dnipro, while also pointing to Russian pressure on Moldova and threats toward Poland and the Baltic states. Russia continues to pour missiles and drones into Ukraine The battlefield campaign has been accompanied by a sustained Russian long-range attack campaign against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Since the beginning of 2026, Russia has launched more than 2,100 missiles against Ukraine, including more than 950 ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy. Ballistic missiles are particularly difficult for Ukraine to counter because it has a limited supply of interceptors capable of engaging them. Russia’s heavy use of ballistic weapons is therefore contributing directly to civilian deaths and infrastructure destruction. Over the first eight months of the year, Russia also used 63,000 attack drones of various types, Zelenskyy said. More than 7,700 were jet-powered Geran drones, which he described as particularly destructive and dangerous. The newer jet-powered drones are faster and more advanced than earlier Shahed-type models, making them harder to intercept and adding to the pressure on Ukraine’s air defenses as Russia attacks cities and infrastructure. Zelenskyy said Russia was using the drones continuously to disrupt economic activity and normal life in Ukrainian cities, including by making it harder for children to attend school. The figures show the scale of the Russian campaign beyond the front line. Alongside its ground offensive, Russia is using sustained missile and drone strikes to kill civilians, destroy infrastructure, and exhaust Ukraine’s air-defense resources. North Korean troops add to Russia’s war effort Zelenskyy also highlighted North Korea’s direct involvement in Russia’s war, saying its troops have suffered heavy losses while gaining battlefield experience alongside Russian forces. He said North Korea’s military capabilities were also benefiting from its cooperation with Russia, pointing to improvements in its ballistic missiles and drone capabilities. Ukraine recently transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Zelenskyy said capturing the soldiers alive had been difficult and described one prisoner’s attempt to take his own life after realizing he was about to be captured. He said the soldiers had been conditioned to believe they had to die rather than surrender. “Do you really want to give such a force more time to learn how to fight?” Zelenskyy asked. Zelenskyy calls for de-escalation before winter Zelenskyy separately warned that Russia could again target Ukraine’s energy and heating infrastructure this winter. Russia has already intensified attacks on Ukraine’s energy system ahead of the cold season. Russia has also explicitly threatened to “freeze” Ukraine this winter, with its Defense Ministry linking the threat to attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. The country spent much of the previous winter dealing with the consequences of Russian strikes on power and heating infrastructure, including blackouts and disruptions to heat supplies. Zelenskyy said Ukraine expects the coming winter to be difficult but warned that if Russia continues attacking Ukraine’s energy and heating systems, Ukraine will make the winter painful for Russia as well. He called for steps toward de-escalation before winter, saying that diplomacy and military strength were both needed to end the war. title: Russia could launch limited attacks on NATO in coming months, escalating hybrid warfare without being ready for full-scale conflict, Denmark warns
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russia is likely to intensify its hybrid war against the West, including more frequent sabotage and cyberattacks that could cause greater damage and casualties, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said in a new assessment published on 24 September. The assessment says Russia has become increasingly willing to take risks against European and NATO countries, even while its full-scale war against Ukraine continues. DDIS also assesses a low but growing risk of Russia carrying out a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia in the coming months. Russia preparing to escalate hybrid attacks DDIS said Russia’s hybrid attacks have increasingly shifted from attempts to create fear and weaken support for Ukraine toward efforts to directly disrupt Western assistance to Kyiv. This includes sabotage targeting defense companies and railway transport carrying military equipment to Ukraine. The Danish intelligence service expects Russia to carry out such attacks more frequently and with greater consequences. Future operations could include destructive cyberattacks capable of disrupting critical societal functions and sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties, according to the assessment. DDIS also cited the foiled drone attack against Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany as an example of Russia’s growing willingness to conduct operations against targets in Europe. German authorities said the attack had been planned by Russia over several months. Explore further Germany suspects Russian intelligence behind arson attack as hybrid warfare threat grows across Europe Growing risk of a limited attack on NATO The Danish intelligence service assesses that there is a low but growing risk Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia. Such an attack could take the form of isolated long-range strikes against infrastructure supporting Ukraine. Russia could also use Ukrainian-made drones in a false-flag operation or deploy a limited number of troops, potentially without national insignia. DDIS says Russia could attempt such an operation even while continuing its war against Ukraine and without having the forces needed for a regional war against NATO. The purpose, according to the assessment, could be to divert European resources away from Ukraine and create divisions within NATO if Moscow believes the alliance would struggle to agree on a collective response. Russia would likely try to ensure that any military attack remained below the threshold that would trigger a full NATO response. DDIS warns, however, that Russia may be uncertain about what would trigger such a response. Explore further After CIA head’s visit to Moscow, Poland’s PM warns Russia is preparing to escalate war. He puts critical window at seven or eight months No signs of an imminent Russian invasion Despite the increased risk of limited attacks, DDIS says it sees no indications that Russia is preparing to invade one or more NATO countries. The agency considers a full-scale Russian invasion of NATO “highly unlikely,” but says it cannot be ruled out. If Russia decided to launch such an invasion, DDIS estimates it would need at least six months to build up the necessary forces. The intelligence service also says Russia would need several months to build up forces near a NATO border before a limited military deployment, making such preparations difficult to conceal. Explore further Russian warship fires flares at Danish military helicopter as Moscow’s provocations escalate Russia under pressure from Ukraine’s attacks The assessment says Russia is currently under more pressure than at any other point in its war against Ukraine. Ukraine’s sustained long-range strikes are causing increasing damage deep inside Russia, while Russian forces are suffering heavy losses for marginal territorial gains. Moscow is also facing economic pressure from military spending, international sanctions and Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure. DDIS assesses that there is no prospect of Russia achieving a major breakthrough in Ukraine over the next six months. At the same time, it says Putin is highly unlikely to compromise on his fundamental objectives in the war. The agency says Russia believes Europe will develop a stronger independent military capability by 2030, which Moscow could view as an increasing threat. This could create what DDIS describes as a window of opportunity for Putin to attempt to change Europe’s security order. title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1674: Eight months of 2026 have brought more Ukrainian civilian casualties than all of last year
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Exclusives Two plants make 70% of Ukraine’s steel. Russia hit both. Then ports closed, rail costs rose 30%, and the EU’s carbon tax kicked in . The head of Ukraine's largest steel plant says the government needs a single rescue document with deadlines and assigned agencies, because each problem stalls when handled alone. Military For the 17th or 18th time, Putin promised to take Donetsk "in a few months" – Zelenskyy . Zelenskyy says Russia has spent nearly five years trying to seize Donetsk, suffering nearly 249,000 troops killed or severely wounded this year for only slightly more than 1,000 square kilometers of territorial gains. He started as a driver. Now he pilots Ukraine's heavy strike drones . He started on the Vampire, then taught himself three more airframes, so when Russian jamming grounds one, he keeps flying on the next. Russia strikes Kyiv with ballistic and hypersonic missiles, damaging maternity hospital amid US-led push for energy truce . US-led efforts to secure a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure are underway. He swore to defend Ukraine, then switched to Russia when it seized Crimea. Twelve years later, Ukrainian FPV drone found him commanding Russian regiment . Colonel Oleksandr Isaiev, a Mykolaiv native who switched to Russia during the seizure of Crimea, died in an FPV drone strike. Ukraine's Vivaldi counteroffensive near Lyman just got help from behind Russian lines: partisans say they cut rail supply to three Russian regiments, no explosion needed . ATESH says it disabled four relay cabinets in Voronezh Oblast, which helped a Russian operation in Donetsk Oblast. Vivaldi erased Russia's Lyman pincer. Now Moscow is pushing toward Sloviansk instead . DeepState says Ukraine stopped one Russian approach to its fortified Donetsk cities. Moscow is pressing another. Ukraine said its troops have kept the routes open. Russian-linked software sold to US government as CEO allegedly hid Russian control – two now arrested . Ukraine put robots where its soldiers used to die clearing mines—and lost none . Sent into kill zones too deadly for people, the machines clear paths, mine enemy routes, and evacuate the wounded. OpenAI hands Ukraine a free AI system to guard its hospitals and power plants from hackers . It runs on its own, spotting flaws in Kyiv's networks and sealing them before intruders slip in, and arrives as Russia keeps striking the same targets by air. Czech journalists caught Rybar operatives posing as documentary filmmakers in Prague, who fled when confronted by reporters from Seznam Zprávy. Year ago, only 12 Ukrainian brigades could order weapons online. Now, 500 units participate in revolutionary program that has delivered 1.3 million drones to front . DOT-Chain Defense lets frontline units order their own drones and gear. Russia is mapping everyday targets across Kyiv, from trolleybus depots to Zhuliany airport, top monitoring channel says, ahead of ballistic strike . It costs about $9,900 and does three other jobs too . The KARA can drop bombs, relay signals, ferry FPV drones to the front, or strike, and it is on sale on Ukraine's state marketplace. A former US nuclear-sub commander, a Ukrainian fund, and a plan to shield Odesa with drone swarms . Ukraine can't fully export its weapons yet, but its battle-tested tech is so in demand that two Ukrainian players just went to Denmark. Old American armor, new Ukrainian brain: Skelya regiment nears completion of M1117 unmanned conversion . The regiment's Innovation Center is finishing a project to remotely control an armored vehicle based on a chassis originally designed during the Vietnam War era. International EU approves nearly €3 billion for Ukraine as Kyiv meets more reform targets . The latest payment brings EU support under the Ukraine Facility to more than €32 billion, while Norway adds €92 million in non-repayable funding. Russian attack puts three countries on alert as drones enter Moldova and Romania . Moldovan police preliminarily identified the drone that exploded beside a farm as a camera-equipped Gerbera, the first of its type found in the country. Russians guard Madagascar's parliament speaker as Moscow builds Indian Ocean foothold – RFE/RL . Russia also trains Madagascar's troops and may recruit workers for drones used against Ukraine. Zelenskyy asks Japan for air-defense technology and offers Ukraine's drones in return, while courting Chile to expand Ukraine's reach in Latin America . Once dependent on donated weapons, Ukraine now trades its battle-tested drone expertise for the protection and partners it still can't supply itself. The drones' small explosive payloads could temporarily close airports or ports without causing widespread destruction, the outlet says. A fresh $42 million, new sanctions, and a seat in the coalition rebuilding Ukraine's Navy. Australia just signed its long-term security pact with Ukraine . The pact bundles weapons, energy, and humanitarian aid, widens sanctions to nearly 1,900 measures, and brings Canberra's total support to nearly $1.3 billion. “Food must never be used as a weapon”: EU calls for Black Sea attack moratorium . The push comes as attacks have made the route increasingly dangerous and costly for commercial shipping, threatening a key trade lifeline for Ukraine and a major source of food for global markets. A senior UN official told the Security Council the toll is worsening as strikes reach cities far from the front, with a dark winter ahead. The diver's lawyers plan to appeal in Croatia and international courts, while Zhuravliov plans to announce an indefinite hunger strike. Read our previous daily review here .

title: US to provide critical but more limited capabilities to NATO, top commander says
body: NATO’s top commander said on Thursday the United States would continue to provide “critical but more limited capabilities” to the alliance as Europeans take up a greater role in defending the continent. U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, was speaking in a phone interview with Reuters en route to a change of command ceremony at a NATO headquarters in Norfolk, Virginia, where a British army general will take over from a U.S. Navy vice admiral. However, NATO recently announced that is stepping up intelligence-sharing in response to a wave of sabotage and other incidents apparently linked to Russia but should be “calm and confident” that it can handle any threat posed by Moscow, the alliance’s top commander told Reuters on Thursday. The comments by US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich came after Denmark’s defense intelligence service warned that Russia was likely to intensify a hybrid war — a term that covers a range of attacks below the level of a conventional military assault — against the West in the coming months. The Danish service added there was “a low but growing risk” that Moscow might launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries that border Russia. “It’s concerning,” Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said of a string of incidents in recent weeks including an attempted drone attack at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport and a Russian ship firing flares towards a Danish military helicopter. “But we should be calm and confident that we as an alliance, the most powerful alliance in history, have the tools that we need and have the mechanisms that we need in order to manage the risk here,” he added. Moscow has repeatedly denied any involvement in hybrid warfare or sabotage operations in NATO countries, or plotting any confrontation. PUTIN BETTER NOT TRY ATTACK ‘ON MY WATCH’, GENERAL SAYS Grynkewich was speaking in a phone interview with Reuters en route to a change-of-command ceremony at a NATO headquarters in Norfolk, Virginia, where a British army general is taking over from a US Navy vice admiral. Asked about the risk of a limited Russian attack on NATO territory, Grynkewich stressed the alliance’s readiness for any such contingency, saying such a development was “unlikely but something that we can’t rule out”. Grynkewich dismissed suggestions that Russian President Vladimir Putin might see an opportunity to strike at NATO, given that the US has used up much of its global stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles in the war with Iran, according to people familiar with the data. “Absolutely not. He better not try it on my watch,” he said, adding NATO was well positioned to defend every inch of its territory. “If we proceed from the phase we’re in and we start to see emerging threats, I’m confident that I have the authorities now that I need in order to take actions to deter any aggression against the alliance.” NATO IN MIDST OF CHANGE AS EUROPEANS TAKE GREATER ROLE The handover of Norfolk to a European commander is part of a broader reshuffle in keeping with US President Donald Trump’s demands that European nations take more responsibility for their own security. It will also see a European taking charge of NATO’s Joint Force Command in Naples. NATO’s Joint Force Command Norfolk is responsible for operations in the Arctic and northern Europe as well as protecting transatlantic resupply routes. Attempting to reassure European allies concerned about an ongoing review of US forces on the continent, Grynkewich said Washington would continue “to provide critical but more limited capabilities” to NATO as Europeans took on a greater role. He said there was “no predetermined outcome” in terms of how many US troops would remain in Europe and “what the capabilities are that might relocate”. About 80,000 US troops are currently based on the continent. Trump has repeatedly threatened to leave NATO, which has been dominated by the US since its establishment in 1949, accusing Europeans of being free-riders on security.

title: France to send military to protect Saudi Arabia on Red Sea oil route, Macron says
body: PARIS, Sept 24 (Reuters) — France will send troops and defense systems to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, which is key for energy transport, French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday. Macron also said a U.S. ban on diesel exports, which the White House has denied is under consideration, would be “catastrophic,” both globally and for the U.S. economy. Macron was speaking in a wide-ranging primetime television interview on the international situation, in which he also warned about possible Russian attacks on French soil. Facing growing pressure at home over high energy prices, Macron sought to assure the French that France had adequate gas and oil supplies as winter approaches. He said Paris was actively working to ensure flows were not disrupted. Crude oil prices have surged recently as the main alternative route for Saudi oil exports through Yanbu has come under missile attacks from Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis. “We are going to send military resources, that is to say, soldiers, radar systems and defense systems, to protect this site — not to get us involved in any conflicts, but to protect this site,” Macron told TF1 and France 2 TV. Russian threat Macron dismissed a report by Spanish newspaper El Mundo that the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency had warned European governments about the threat of potential drone attacks from the Mediterranean. “I can deny it. The CIA did not inform French services,” he said. Still, Macron said Russia is multiplying hostile and criminal acts against European countries, and France could face strikes similar to the failed attack in Leipzig. Germany said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack in August on the Leipzig airport. Macron gathered French party chiefs at the Elysee last week to brief them on the growing threat from Russia. He later said he had ordered his government to draw up a plan to protect critical infrastructure against drone and cyber attacks. Macron said Moscow was seeking to intimidate Europe and break the continent’s resolve in supporting Ukraine. Russia says European allegations of hybrid attacks are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria. Yet Macron’s position on Russia was weakened this week after France shocked other EU members by getting Russian-Uzbek metals tycoon Alisher Usmanov exempted from EU sanctions, citing national security concerns. That prompted Azerbaijan to pardon a French national jailed for espionage.

title: Bomb Markings On Thai F-16s Shed New Light On Cambodia Combat Operations
body: Mission markings appearing on Royal Thai Air Force F-16s offer new clues about the weapons and aircraft employed during the 2025 fighting with Cambodia, which also saw the Gripen’s combat debut and strikes involving T-50THs. In the summer of 2025, a border incident broke out between the two Southeast Asian countries of Thailand and Cambodia . An armed confrontation had already occurred on May 28, 2025, before much wider fighting broke out in July . The brief conflict was followed by a wider air and ground clash in December. Thai ground forces were supported by the air force in large numbers and with various types of aircraft both around the border and in the Cambodian hinterland. RTAF F-16 with AMRAAM, IRIS-T and GBU-12. | Source: RTAF The border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand stems from the ambiguity of the border demarcations established under the 1904 and 1907 agreements, which were made during the demarcation of the border between the Kingdom of Siam (now Thailand) and the French Third Republic, along the border with French Indochina. After Cambodia gained independence from France in 1953, the sovereignty of the Preah Vihear temple complex became a focus of dispute. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) issued a ruling in 1962, awarding the temple itself to Cambodia, citing historical maps and French survey documentation. However, disputes remained over the surrounding territory. In 2013, following a request by Cambodia for an interpretation of the 1962 judgment, the ICJ clarified that its earlier ruling had awarded Cambodia sovereignty over the entire promontory of Preah Vihear and required Thailand to withdraw its personnel from that territory. The ruling did not resolve sovereignty over other disputed areas outside the promontory, and broader sections of the border remained contested. The dispute remained largely dormant until the end of the 20th century. Between 2008 and 2011, military clashes flared up again, including artillery clashes, border guard incidents, and limited incursions, resulting in several deaths and injuries on both sides. These clashes highlighted the persistent instability and challenges in the region. A key incident that further escalated tensions occurred on July 23, 2025, when soldiers from the Thai 14th Infantry Battalion stepped on a landmine in Nam Yuen District, Ubon Ratchathani Province. The incident left five Thai soldiers injured, with one losing his right leg. The Thai Foreign Ministry issued a statement strongly condemning the incident, saying newly laid mines violated Thailand’s sovereignty and the Ottawa Convention on the Prohibition of Anti-Personnel Mines. Cambodia rejected the accusation that it had laid new mines, saying the incident occurred in an existing minefield inside Cambodian territory. The situation quickly escalated into armed conflict following the mine incident. The air force was immediately put on alert. In the south, the 7th Wing’s Gripen jets in Surat Thani Province relocated some of its aircraft to the north at Korat Air Base , 130 km (80 mi) from the border, where F-16s of the 1st Wing, including 103rd Squadron, are also based. The initial clashes lasted five days, but the Thai Air Force acknowledged that its aircraft had carried out several bombing raids against Cambodian forces. It was then that the news broke that the Gripen had carried out its first combat strikes. This was not only the first time in Thai service, but also the first known combat employment of the type itself. Although Swedish Gripens participated in the 2011 Libyan conflict, they only carried out reconnaissance missions there from Sicily. Another clash began on Dec. 7-8, 2025, lasted for weeks, and saw more intensive air and ground operations from both sides. On Dec. 9, 2025, the Air Force’s JAS 39 Gripen fighters carried out an airstrike on a casino opposite the Chong Chom border crossing in Surin Province, Cambodia. This happened after the casino was reportedly used by the Cambodian army to launch attack drones, as a hideout for BM-21 Grad 122 mm rocket launchers, and as a troop staging point, according to the Thai military. On the evening of Dec. 10, 2025, F-16 fighter jets carried out an airstrike, dropping bombs on a casino building in the Chub Ko Kee area of Banteay Ampil district, Cambodia. In addition, Thai troops provided artillery support for an attack on a Cambodian oil depot opposite the Sai Taku border crossing in Ban Kruat district, Buriram Province. The attack came after the Thai side claimed that the casino and oil depot were being used by Cambodian forces as military facilities, including as a site for attack drone operations against Thai soldiers and as a storage facility for heavy weapons and BM-21 rockets. Cambodian BM-21 GRAD. | Source: Tang Chhin Sothy / AFP On the morning of Dec. 12, 2025, the Thai military reported the successful destruction of military targets opposite Chanthaburi and Trat provinces, supported by airstrikes to weaken Cambodian forces. Estimated Cambodian losses, according to the Thai side, were nine armored vehicles and tanks, 68 drones, one counter-drone system, three communication towers, and one BM-21 multiple launch rocket system. F-16 fighter jets also attacked ground targets, dropping GBU-12 Paveway II laser-guided bombs on what the Thai military described as a Cambodian army warehouse storing BM-21 rockets and heavy weapons. At 5:45 a.m. on Dec. 13, 2025, a reporter monitoring the situation at Ban Chamrak, Mueang District, Trat Province, on the Thai-Cambodian border reported that two F-16 fighter jets began bombing targets around the Chai Chum Neang Bridge in Pursat Province, Cambodia. The first bombing occurred at 5:51 a.m., and the fifth and final one at 6:12 a.m. The first two attacks targeted a nearby casino building, while the final rounds targeted the Chai Chum Neang Bridge and a bridge parallel to it, about 5 km from the border. The attacks reportedly damaged both river crossings, disrupting the transport of military equipment from the Cambodian side. The casino building was also damaged. Casino gambling is prohibited in Thailand, so in recent years casinos have been built on the other side of the border, in Cambodia. Many of the buildings are located immediately beyond Cambodian border crossings and cater heavily to Thai and foreign customers. The destruction of the Thmodah Casino | Source: RTAF On Dec. 15, 2025, F-16s carried out an airstrike, bombing Cambodian arms and ammunition depots located approximately 72 kilometers from the Thai border in Preah Netr Preah district, Banteay Meanchey Province. During the morning of Dec. 15, 2025, F-16s dropped two bombs on a building complex in Poipet, Banteay Meanchey Province, known for its casino tourism. The Thai Air Force said the operation was in a suburban area and did not target civilians, while Cambodian authorities and media reported damage to a civilian warehouse, claiming that it was bombed by Thai forces. Royal Thai Air Force spokesman Maj. Gen. Chakrit Thamvichai said the operation targeted an ammunition depot used to stockpile BM-21 rockets, which Cambodia had used to attack Thai civilians the previous night. Cambodian buildings destruction at Preah Netr Preah. | Source: RTAF The spokesman said, “Prior to the attack, the Thai military conducted intelligence gathering to confirm that the target was military. We observed activity around the building, including the loading of BM-21 rockets, which led us to conclude that the target was legitimate for the attack. We detected secondary explosions at various points, indicating the destruction of BM-21 rockets that were stored in that area,” Chakrit explained, showing video footage of the operation at a press conference. On Dec. 18, 2025, images posted on Cambodian social media showed the wreckage of a Thai unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), with Cambodian sources claiming that it had been shot down. The downed UAV was a DP-20. Thai authorities subsequently confirmed the loss but said the aircraft had lost control at approximately 8:00 p.m. on Dec. 17, 2025, with its last signal detected about 10 km east of Poipet. According to Thailand’s Joint Press Center, the DP-20 was developed by Thailand’s Defence Technology Institute and was still in the research and testing phase, supporting Royal Thai Army operations. Thai authorities said the cause of the loss remained under investigation. DP20 MALE UAV | Source: DTI On Dec. 21, 2025, a Royal Thai Air Force Aerostar BP unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) crashed in Banteay Meanchey, opposite Sa Kaeo Province. Cambodian forces claimed to have shot down the aircraft. The Aerostar BP has been in service with Thailand for about 10 years, used by the air force for surveillance and reconnaissance, and is currently stationed with the 3rd Wing’s 301st Squadron in Watthana Nakhon. On Dec. 24, 2025, it was reported that KAI T-50TH aircraft had been deployed to attack Cambodian targets. On the same day, an F-16 fighter jet dropped bombs on a Cambodian fortified command post near Phnom Chearach Mountain. Finally, on Dec. 27, 2025, Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire agreement, ending 20 days of fighting along their border over territorial claims. The ceasefire took effect at noon local time. In Thailand, Children’s Day is celebrated nationwide on the second Saturday of January. For this occasion, the Thai armed forces, including the air force, hold open days and flying displays at many of their bases. During the event held on the military side of Bangkok’s Don Mueang International Airport, the F-16 aircraft with Thai registration number 10311 (serial number 87-0707) from 103rd Squadron flew a spectacular display. But it was not this, but the markings painted on the left side of the aircraft, under the cockpit, that attracted the attention of the audience. Here, bomb silhouettes could be seen, which would indicate that the aircraft flew combat missions during the Cambodian conflict. Under the three Lizard laser-guided bomb markings, several Mk.82 and Mk.84 icons could also be made out. The mission markings have been appearing on the sides of several aircraft in recent months on social media platforms of various Thai armed forces pages, including the Air Force, and in photos posted by several civilian photographers. So far, a total of 19 Thai F-16s have been identified with various bomb icons (Mk.82, Mk.84, Lizard/GBU-12), including aircraft from 103rd Squadron, which flies F-16A/B Block 15 OCU (Operational Capability Upgrade) aircraft, and, more recently, 403rd Squadron, which operates F-16A/B Block 15 aircraft upgraded to the MLU standard. Thailand’s first batch of 12 aircraft (eight F-16As and four F-16Bs) arrived in Thailand in 1988. In September 1995, Thailand received the first aircraft from a second shipment of 18 Block 15 OCU aircraft, 12 A-models and six B-models. These were used to form a second F-16 squadron based in Thailand. The last six F-16s were delivered in February 1996 and were among the last new-build Block 15 aircraft produced. On July 14, 2000, the Thai government decided to purchase 16 used F-16s (15 A-models and one B-model), including former U.S. Air Force ADF variants, to form a third squadron. On Nov. 18, 2004, it was announced that Thailand would receive seven former Singapore F-16A/Bs (three A- and four B-models), which were delivered in 2005. Instead of a government-to-government purchase, these aircraft were donated to the air force by the Singaporean government as part of an arrangement connected with Singapore’s use of Thai airspace and training areas. By the 2000s, many of the aircraft were approaching their 20th year of service, so a Mid-Life Upgrade (MLU) program was initiated for 18 aircraft assigned to 403rd Squadron. The MLU program was intended to extend the aircraft’s capabilities and service life, which was a more cost-effective solution than purchasing new aircraft. For the modernization, the air force commissioned Thai Aviation Industries (TAI), in collaboration with Lockheed Martin, in three phases, with six aircraft per phase, so a total of 18 aircraft underwent the program during the 2010s. The MLU included the new AN/APG-68(V)9 radar, AMRAAM capability, improved IFF equipment, an upgraded countermeasures system, the Link 16 encrypted data communications system, and the JHMCS (Joint Helmet Mounted Cueing System). The last six aircraft were delivered to 403rd Squadron on Sept. 24, 2018. Delivery of the first F-16 MLU. | Source: RTAF As for the bombing, it is worth mentioning that on the two-seat aircraft with serial number 10304, in addition to the 16 Mk.82 icons, a KGGB icon could also be seen. The KGGB (Korean GPS Guided Bomb) is a guided glide bomb system that can be attached to the Mk.82 conventional general-purpose bomb. The KGGB is capable of hitting targets from long distances and has a fire-and-forget capability. It was developed by South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development and LIG Nex1. It was officially announced in November 2023 that the Thai Air Force had adopted the KGGB. Although the number was not officially disclosed, Janes reported that the RTAF had ordered 20 KGGB kits in two batches of 10 in 2022. F-16 serial 10311 with bomb marks. | Source: RTAF The KGGB is a precision-guided munition (PGM) equipped with GPS/INS guidance. It integrates a Global Positioning System (GPS) and an Inertial Navigation System (INS), enabling effective operation regardless of the time of day and providing a degree of resilience in degraded navigation environments. What makes the bomb interesting is that it was designed to minimize the additional aircraft integration required. Basically, an aircraft already capable of carrying the Mk.82 can potentially employ the weapon with comparatively limited modifications. This may be why the KGGB was visible on older South Korean F-5 and F-4 aircraft and was dropped during testing. A portable touchscreen tablet is used as part of the weapon’s cockpit interface. According to Korean sources, it can engage targets at ranges of up to around 100 km, depending on launch conditions. Weapons option for the 103th squadron. | Source: RTAF In addition to the F-16s, bomb silhouette images have also been released from the new KAI T-50TH Golden Eagle and the old F-5TH aircraft. On the latter two, only Mk.82 icons were visible, despite the fact that the F-5E/F Tiger II aircraft were recently modernized. The Air Force’s F-5E/F fighter is a third-generation, twin-engine, supersonic light fighter-bomber, acquired in two phases under the Peace Rama program beginning in the late 1970s. Although the aircraft were modernized once in 2000 (multifunction display, HOTAS control system, Python-4 air-to-air missile), by the 21st century the type had limited capabilities and, for example, lacked a modern beyond-visual-range air-to-air capability. Due to Thailand’s economic constraints, acquiring another Gripen squadron to replace the remaining F-5s was not pursued at the time, so the Air Force instead expanded the capabilities of the existing aircraft. In 2018, an upgrade program was launched using Israeli technology, during which the F-5T Tiger aircraft of the 21st Wing, 211th Squadron, were modernized to the F-5TH standard. Thai F-5, with 20 Mk.82 bomb marks | Source: RTAF The F-5TH received a modern mission computer (MC) for more efficient data processing. A color moving map and two multifunction color displays (MFCD) were installed in the cockpit. In addition, it received upgraded communications equipment, an improved head-up display (HUD), and a digital video and data recorder (DVDR) system, as well as a post-flight evaluation system (Debriefing System). The aircraft’s electrical and environmental control system (ECS), including its associated systems, was further improved. The aircraft’s central component, the old radar, was also replaced with the ELTA Systems ELM-2032 multimode pulse-Doppler radar. The Israeli radar has different operating modes, including air-to-air, air-to-ground and maritime modes. As for armament, it can employ modern missiles currently in service with the Air Force, such as the American AIM-9M Sidewinder, the Israeli Python-4 and the European IRIS-T. With a helmet-mounted sight, high-off-boresight missiles can be aimed at the target using the pilot’s line of sight. For targets beyond visual range (BVR), it can carry the I-Derby air-to-air missile. The Elbit Lizard III laser-guided bombs have also been added to the weapons kit and can be guided to their target using a targeting pod. The Lizard is a semi-active laser guidance kit for aerial bombs developed and manufactured by Israel’s Elbit Systems. The kit can be fitted to conventional general-purpose bombs, transforming them into precision weapons. Essentially, it can be considered an Israeli counterpart to the American Paveway concept. The Sky Shield electronic warfare pod, also developed in Israel, has also been added to the aircraft. The pod detects enemy radars and is capable of suppressing integrated air defense surveillance and fire-control radars using electronic countermeasures. With the Link-T data link system, the aircraft is able to communicate with other aircraft, ground control points, and airborne early warning and control aircraft. The Royal Thai Air Force ordered 14 T-50TH trainer and light-attack aircraft for the 4th Wing, 401st Squadron, at Takhli Air Base. They replaced the old Aero Vodochody L-39ZA/ART Albatros trainer aircraft, which were retired at the end of March 2021. A total of 36 aircraft initially entered service in the 1990s, with four more subsequently acquired, and their weapons systems and avionics were upgraded by Israel’s Elbit in the 2000s. The Air Force initially required 50-60 L-39 aircraft for five squadrons, but this was reduced due to economic considerations. The T-50TH s, according to statements made during the development of the fleet, were also planned to receive Thailand’s Link-T data link network system and additional weapons and targeting capabilities. The type’s light-attack capability became particularly relevant during the December 2025 conflict, when T-50THs were reported to have been employed against Cambodian targets.

title: Royal Air Force Secretly Jamming Adversary Satellites Over Past Year
body: The Royal Air Force has been jamming satellites from adversary nations in order to defend British national interests, including its nuclear deterrent. This was revealed by the BBC on Sept. 23, 2026, on the first day of the UK’s Space Power Conference . They report that the RAF has been using a ground based system to disrupt satellites used by adversary nations for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) against the UK’s critical defence infrastructure. These satellites are used to track the movements of critical defence assets, including the UK’s continuous at sea nuclear deterrent, through a combination of high resolution imagery, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and as of yet unknown methods and sensors. Satellites monitoring the Royal Navy’s Vanguard class nuclear ballistic missile submarines (SSBN) put the deterrent at risk as information gathered by satellite can allow a hostile actor to locate the submarine and disable it, preventing the UK from utilising its second-strike capabilities during a time of crisis. With Russia’s rhetoric surrounding its own nuclear stockpile, ongoing since the beginning of the invasion of Ukraine, it is imperative that the UK’s nuclear deterrent cannot fail. UK has been jamming satellites from other countries to defend itself from hostile threats, BBC told https://t.co/OcuELAPWdF — BBC Breaking News (@BBCBreaking) September 23, 2026 This news comes as the RAF has set up its first dedicated space defence squadron, named No. III Space Effects Squadron , which is tasked with “disrupting, degrading and denying hostile threats in space.” It is unclear if this squadron will be responsible for further use of the ground based jamming system against hostile ISR satellites. This squadron will also be essential in defending the UK’s space assets, upon which the nation is extremely reliant. UK and commercial satellites provide the country with mobile phone data, weather forecasts and online ordering, whilst Global Positioning System (GPS) provide critical navigation to the general public and emergency services. For the UK, defence-orientated satellites provide intelligence gathering and missile warning capabilities that help to give the Armed Forces an edge during warfighting. The defence of these satellites is just as vital to the country as the defence of the nuclear deterrent, so the official standing up of this squadron is good news for British security. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting making the announcement about the RAF’s jamming of hostile satellites to defend UK defence assets. | Source: UK Space Power Conference In his keynote speech at the UK Space Power Conference on Wednesday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting emphasised that “two Russian satellites had intercepted the communications of at least a dozen European ones since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.” Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries. My message at the Space Power Conference 2026. pic.twitter.com/4w3ZhEiY7k — Wes Streeting (@wesstreeting) September 24, 2026 Showing that “not only do our adversaries have the capability to threaten our national interests and national security, they also unsurprisingly have the intent and that requires us to act.” Regarding No III squadron, Streeting stated that it will have “the ability to conduct offensive and defensive operations, to strengthen deterrence, reduce opportunities for coercion and enhance the resilience of our space capabilities.” RAF Chief of the Air Staff Sir Harv Smyth giving his keynote speech at the UK Space Power Conference. | Source: UK Space Power Conference The Chief of the Air Staff (CAS), Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, reiterated the importance of space during his keynote speech, stating that “Space is no longer just simply supporting air power from the sidelines. It is completely embedded within it… The effective use of space is critical to the ability of our new integrated force to understand, to communicate, to move and to fight.” He added that “Space is obviously a prerequisite for modern air power. Every element of a sixth-generation air force depends intimately on space, the networks, the targeting, the navigation, the command and control.” The first UK Space Power Conference has started. It’s a packed house and agenda as the UK looks to deliver its new Space Strategy. Space is an essential element of National resilience, and the Conference will discuss how we ensure its security and exploit its advantages. pic.twitter.com/tehrfXfCji — Greg Bagwell (@gregbagwell) September 23, 2026 This renewed focus on space power comes as the RAF’s headquarters at RAF High Wycombe was redesignated as Air and Space Command, reflecting the integration of space within the RAF. This follows a familiar trend across the world as air forces rebrand themselves to better reflect the new reality of 21st Century warfighting. To match this name change and the renewed importance of space, the British government announced in the 2026 Defence Investment Plan that £9 billion of new space capability would be made available for the 2030 to 2035 period. This comes alongside investments, from this year up to 2030, of £2.3 billion for satellite communications, £880 million for space-based ISR and space control and “£440 million for novel space technology.” Space Deterrence and the UK The Defence Secretary and the CAS both emphasised in their speeches the importance of deterrence in space and that is worth discussing here. A good working definition of space deterrence comes from Eugene C. Richter, a Lt Colonel in the US Air Force, in his research paper to the U.S. Air War College Air University in 2024. He describes the concept as focusing “on how to deter attacks on capabilities within the space domain, not necessarily on the use of space-enabled means to deter aggression.” It concerns dissuading an adversary from taking hostile measures to “deny, degrade, disrupt, or destroy one’s space assets and capabilities” which act as a core enabler for the air, land and sea domains of warfare. Without space certain capabilities are reduced in their effectiveness, or in some ways stopped entirely. A STARLINK satellite in orbit, in front of the M101 galaxy captured by the British Noctis-1 military telescope, which monitors objects in Earth’s orbit, providing position information on UK satellites, helping to prevent collisions and protecting critical space assets. | Source: Crown copyright 2026/MOD The Russo-Ukrainian war demonstrates this concept, with Russian forces using Starlink, terminals taken through third party sources, to provide battlefield communication for troops and drones. Once SpaceX was able to prevent Russian use of their satellites, it helped Ukraine to blunt several Russian advances in February 2026 . On the other hand Russia’s use of GPS jamming has prevented Ukraine from getting the most out of its US supplied JDAM munitions, which typically rely GPS on for their extremely accurate targeting. New speaker alert Major Gen. (retd.) Paul Tedman, former Commander of UK Space Command, will join FASI’s upcoming online panel discussion to explore the implications of the UK Government’s Defence Investment Plan for air & space power. 1 Oct https://t.co/QZL9CjiP1c pic.twitter.com/RxxBU2mIX9 — Freeman Air and Space Institute (@freeman_air) September 22, 2026 Deterring adverse space activity such as this is central to establishing military dominance on the 21st century battlefield and, as a result, this has become a significant focus for military theorists. Interestingly, the Freeman Air and Space Institute , based at King’s College London and set up jointly with the RAF, is placing increasing emphasis on space power over air power due to the nature of modern war becoming reliant on the space domain. Whilst they still provide excellent analysis on the use of air power they have been central to putting space research into government. A computer generated image of the Skynet 5D satellite in orbit. A satellite which provides secure military communications for the UK Armed Forces which was successfully launched in December 2012. | Source: Astrium For budgetary reasons however, discussions about space for the UK have often been theoretical, due to the lack of investment in previous years towards space capabilities. The UK does not currently possess a domestic rocket launching capability, with the British government reliant on commercial actors such as SpaceX , or allies within the European Space Agency for the deployment of satellites. Likewise UK sovereign military satellite capability is limited to the Skynet 5 series of four satellites used for secure communications. Skynet 5 will eventually be replaced by a singular Skynet 6A satellite and a mixture of allied and commercial satellites used within a flexible systems architecture. It is clear from @airpowerassn UK Space Power 2026 that the UK needs to have a sovereign launch capability and the delays in the UK’s 1st space launch at @SaxaVord_Space are concerning many. Speaking to Baroness Lloyd later she said it is a key component of UK space strategy,… — Mark Piesing (@MarkPiesing) September 24, 2026 Fortunately, the UK may gain a sovereign space launch capability through various horizontal and vertical spaceports around the UK, but progress here has been slow. It is noteworthy that the last attempt to launch a space vehicle from the UK failed to reach space and resulted in the closure of Virgin Orbit , the company that made the attempt. ‘Cosmic Girl’, a customised 747-400 aircraft, seen here carrying the test launch vehicle. The company said that an anomaly meant the rocket could not reach the required altitude and was later lost forcing the company to declare bankruptcy in the aftermath. | Source: Crown copyright 2021/VirginOrbit Therefore, the setting up of No. III Space Effects Squadron is a change in how the UK views space, going from a passive position to one in which the UK can achieve direct influence. Their ability to conduct offensive space operations, as well as defensive, allows the UK to become more confident in a domain that is increasingly dominated by the US, Russia and China. Day Two of #UKSpacePower26 is delivering a clear message: Space is central to our #NationalResilience , security and economic growth. Dicussions chaired by Prof Anu Ojha @spacegovuk continue online: https://t.co/b1rZ4vttIl pic.twitter.com/w99HNCFbcq — The Air & Space Power Association (@airpowerassn) September 24, 2026 According to the CAS, squadron numbers IV, V and VI will include a Space Tactics and Training Squadron as well as a squadron which will deliver a deep space advanced radar capability. They will then be joined by a Space Defence function working as part of the newly established Integrated Air, Space and Missile Defence Operations Centre. These will reinforce the pre-existing No. I Space Operations Squadron and No. II Space Warning Squadron which already monitors space for threats, including hostile satellites and space debris. U.S. Space Weapons The revelation that the UK is conducting anti-satellite operations follows the U.S. move last week to reveal that they have secretly deployed weapons into space . Whilst speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference last Monday, the U.S. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said “on orbit” weapons had been deployed and that they were necessary to safeguard U.S. forces against hostile enemy action. He did not reveal what this weapon was, nor how long it has been deployed in space. Theorists are unsure if it is a kinetic kill weapon, an electronic warfare weapon or a laser/radiowave based weapon, but currently this is all speculation. Space weapons can provide a deterrent value preventing other actors from interfering in a nation’s space activities. However, the U.S. commitment to space control, a step beyond simple deterrence, adds another factor to events going on in that domain. According to a U.S. Space Force spokesperson, the U.S. is committed to “contesting and controlling the space domain by employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities through disruption, degradation and even destruction.” Last week marked the first time a US official has acknowledged that it possesses space-based weapons. An arms race in space has been underway for years, writes Mallory Stewart. The important question is why the US chose to make this disclosure now. https://t.co/Bb2oPkSpEc — Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (@BulletinAtomic) September 22, 2026 China responded the day after the announcement, warning against an “arms race” in space, with Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun stating that “We urge the U.S. ​to stop expanding military build-up in outer space, and ⁠uphold global strategic stability with concrete actions.” China itself launched a SC-19 ASAT in 2007 to shoot down the FengYun-1C satellite, at a range of 865 kilometers, which exploded into a large debris field that, according to the ESA , “increased the trackable space object population by 25%.” As of February 2026, 2,351 pieces of this debris still remain in orbit. These weapon systems remain in the Chinese missile arsenal and have been continuously tested throughout the 2010s. Russia similarly launched an ASAT in November 2021, shooting down the defunct Kosmos-1408 satellite that was located in low Earth orbit (LEO). The missile hit the satellite at a range of 650–680km and created a cloud of over 1,500 pieces of trackable orbital debris. According to NASA the situation was so dangerous the crew of the International Space Station (ISS) were forced to shelter in the space station’s multiple Soyuz modules used to return the crew to Earth in an emergency. That this launch occurred mere months before Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine cannot be missed, showing that Russia did this to deliberately send a message to the West about how it would respond to involvement in their war of aggression. Luckily Russia’s threat was never carried out, but the risk of escalation in space remains high. F-15A 76-0086 carrying a centerline CASM-135 ASAT missile. The CASM-135 was the captive version of the ASM-135 missile used during the famous missile test. It is unknown what space weapons the U.S. currently possesses, but they could resemble some conventional weapons already seen on Earth, i.e missiles or air defence lasers. | Source: United States Air Force The U.S. too has launched ASATs against target satellites, and notably fired them from specially modified F-15A fighters . More recently, in 2008, the USS Lake Erie shot a modified SM-3 at a U.S. satellite that was de-orbiting, in what is viewed as a direct response to the Chinese missile test. The operation, known as “Burnt Frost,” did not produce much debris as the satellite was already falling to Earth when it was hit, although the test was controversial at the time. Interestingly, the British government is committed to not testing destructive anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons due to the harm they cause to the rest of the space ecosystem through the creation of long-lived debris fields that threaten other satellites and space vehicles. Space debris is a significant threat to the further development of space with a number of private companies such as Astroscale and ClearSpace working on the safe disposal of satellites and debris, returning it to the planet. Whilst the 1967 Outer Space Treaty explicitly bans nuclear weapons and other types of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) in space, it does not ban conventional weapons, allowing for the weaponisation of space in ways that haven’t been seen before. These worrying developments will have dire consequences for world stability should future conflicts between these powers arise.

title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine has agreed on a new Patriot interceptor package—won’t say with whom
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine has agreed on a new package of Patriot interceptor missiles with an unnamed partner, Suspilne reported . He made the announcement on 24 September during a meeting with the Ukrainian community in the United States. Zelenskyy did not reveal the partner's identity, the quantity, or the delivery timeline. Russia's aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities is heading into its most dangerous winter yet, with ballistic strikes on hospitals, power stations, and residential buildings pushing monthly civilian casualties to their highest level since the war's opening weeks. The gap between the interceptors Ukraine needs and what allies have so far committed has become a central factor in both the defense of Ukrainian cities and the diplomatic standoff. What Zelenskyy said Zelenskyy made the announcement during a broader address to the diaspora about diplomacy, the peace effort, and cooperation with US President Donald Trump's team. "We agreed today—I won't say with whom—on a package of [interceptor] missiles for Patriot systems. This is an important decision," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Ukrainian diaspora in New York. He gave no further details. Zelenskyy said ending the war was the most important question facing Ukraine and awarded decorations to community members who had contributed to the country's defense. Before the New York trip, the interceptor question had been raised with several partners. After meeting Trump on 22 September, Zelenskyy said he had asked Washington for a winter package of Patriot interceptors. That same week, he pitched Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on air-defense cooperation, noting that Mitsubishi Heavy Industries runs the only plant outside the US licensed to assemble PAC-3 missiles. Suspilne noted the issue had also been discussed with other partners Zelenskyy did not name. Intercepting more, but not enough On 24 September, air defenses intercepted 60% of the ballistic missiles Russia fired at Kyiv—a figure the president called significant. "It was 60%—not 10% and not zero. And this year we had moments when it was zero. Not because someone lacks experience, but because someone lacks missiles," Zelenskyy told journalists in New York. Since 12 August, Ukraine's Air Force has stopped publishing detailed figures on how many missiles Russia launches, reporting only what it downs—which makes Zelenskyy's percentage a rare public benchmark. By that count, Russia has fired at least 794 ballistic missiles at Ukraine since January, about 43% of all missiles used this year, with July's 174 the monthly high. The overnight attack Hours after Zelenskyy spoke in New York, Russia launched 295 drones at Ukraine overnight on 24–25 September. In Odesa, Russian drones killed two people—a 40-year-old woman and a 51-year-old man—and injured two others. In Kyiv, Shaheds struck high-rises in Solomianskyi district, and strikes across the broader region killed a 14-year-old boy. Explore further 1,000 Patriot missiles arrive too late for this winter, so Ukraine asked the Ramstein arms coalition to open its warehouses Romania scrambled jets as drones drifted toward its airspace. A woman was injured in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, and the morning brought further Russian strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Poltava , injuring two more people. The interceptor crisis Zelenskyy's announcement lands in the middle of a worsening shortage. In August, he told CNN that Ukraine held roughly 1% of American Patriot stocks and that 5% would get Kyiv through the winter. ISW assessed the same month that the interceptor shortage was one reason Russia saw no incentive to negotiate. The EU has moved to fill the gap. Brussels cleared Ukraine to spend loan money on Patriot missiles and later released €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) for interceptors and drones. But Ukraine's air force commander warned that newly ordered missiles would arrive too late for this winter and asked the Ramstein coalition to open existing stockpiles. At least one partner has now moved from discussion to commitment. The quantity and delivery date remain unknown, and Russia produces ballistic missiles faster than Ukraine's allies have so far been willing to part with the interceptors that stop them. This is an important decision," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Ukrainian diaspora in New York. "It was 60%—not 10% and not zero. And this year we had moments when it was zero. Not because someone lacks experience, but because someone lacks missiles," Zelenskyy told journalists in New York.

title: Ukraine’s Mirage had killed a cruise missile on its first combat sortie. France just sent more of the missiles that reach 80 km
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); France delivered additional MICA air-to-air missiles and 30mm cannon ammunition for Ukraine's Mirage 2000 fighter jets, Militarnyi reported , citing France's Armed Forces Ministry. Delivering an aircraft is one step, keeping it armed is another. France's weapons resupply reflects a shift from one-off hardware transfers to sustained combat support as Russia's aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities grinds on. What MICA does The MICA, developed by MBDA, comes in two versions: radar-guided (MICA RF) and infrared (MICA IR). It weighs about 112 kg, flies at Mach 4.9—nearly five times the speed of sound—and can engage targets 60 to 80 km away. Ukraine's Mirages have also carried older Magic 2 missiles limited to roughly 20 km. MICAs were reportedly included with the original donation, but the supply may have been limited, which would explain why the Magic 2s stayed in use . MICA triples to quadruples that engagement window, letting pilots intercept cruise missiles far earlier in their flight path. The fresh delivery keeps Ukraine's small fleet supplied with the missiles that make these longer-range interceptions possible. Explore further Ukraine is running short of its best missiles for hunting Russia’s jet drones. Now MiG-29s are firing 1970s weapons Cheap shells for cheap drones The 30mm ammunition feeds the Mirage's two built-in DEFA 554 cannons, which fire at a selectable rate of 1,200 or 1,800 rounds per minute. A pilot who uses the gun on a Shahed drone saves a MICA for a target that actually needs one. Ukraine's F-16 operations follow a similar logic: pilots use their 20mm Vulcan cannons alongside AIM-9 and AIM-120 missiles, though Zelenskyy called the missile option expensive—used when nothing else can reach a jet drone, because "a human life is more important." A Ukrainian Mirage 2000 shot down a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile during its very first combat mission, on 7 March 2025. France has delivered about a dozen modified Mirage 2000-5F jets since February 2025, and the fleet is still growing . Read also Ukraine Loses Mirage 2000 In Crash Ukraine’s Swedish radar planes have flown inside Russian missile range for six months. None has been shot down.
